beats.say: Inside every modern NVMe SSD hides a brutal physical trap. Update one tiny record in place, and random four-kilobyte writes smash into massive four-megabyte flash erase blocks — multiplying disk wear ten to thirty times. Watch how LSM-trees turn that random chaos into pure sequential gold.

scenes.title: Pages, erase blocks, and FTL storms

beats.say: Flash silicon obeys an asymmetric law. You can read or write a four-kilobyte page in microseconds, but you can never overwrite a single byte in place. To reclaim space, the SSD must wipe an entire four-megabyte erase block at once.

So the Flash Translation Layer remaps every update to a fresh page and marks the old one stale. Under random updates, dead tombstones scatter everywhere — triggering garbage collection storms that copy live data over and over.

Classic B-Trees were built for spinning disks, updating keys in place. Every write walks down the tree to a scattered sixteen-kilobyte leaf page, mutates a hundred bytes, and marks the whole page dirty.
When millions of random keys churn across the drive, the B-Tree sprays tiny dirty pages across every erase block — hitting the write-amplification wall and choking random IOPS.

An LSM-tree flips the entire game. Incoming writes land straight into a blazing in-memory MemTable, then flush sequentially into immutable sorted tables stacked in a three-dimensional pyramid from Level zero down to Level three.

Background leveled compaction sweeps sorted runs cleanly downward, eliminating random flash fragmentation. And what about reads? Ten-bit Bloom filters guard every table like laser gates — short-circuiting ninety-nine percent of miss lookups before they ever touch disk.

No storage engine escapes the RUM tradeoff: reads, updates, and memory always pull against each other. B-Trees win on predictable point reads; LSM-trees crush write-heavy streams on flash. Know the silicon underneath, and turn random writes into sequential streams.
